en: Parivāra 3.
Summary of the Headings on Origination (Samuṭṭhānasīsa-saṅkhepa) 1.
Summary Verse on Origination (Samuṭṭhāna-uddāna)
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
suffering, and non-self;
so too are nibbāna and designations.
"Non-self"— this is the firm conviction.
When the moon of the Buddha has not yet arisen,
and the sun of the Buddha has not yet ascended;
Of those things that share a common nature,
not even the mere name is known.
Having performed various difficult deeds,
Having fulfilled the perfections,
the great heroes arise as the very eyes for the world including the Brahmās.
They teach the true Dhamma,
which brings about the destruction of suffering and leads to happiness—
the Aṅgīrasa, the Sakyan Sage.
Compassionate toward all beings,
the Lion, supreme among all creatures,
taught the three Piṭakas.
The Suttanta, the Abhidhamma,
and the Vinaya of great merit—
thus is the True Dhamma maintained.
If the Vinaya remains,
it consists of both Vibhaṅgas,
the Khandhakas, and the Mātikā.
Just as a garland is strung together by the quality of its thread,
so too is one bound by one's retinue; [one should therefore cultivate] that very retinue.
The origin is fixed and accomplished;
further, the schism and its cause are seen in the Sutta above.
Therefore, one who loves the Dhamma and is truly well-behaved should train in its retinue. 2.
Thirteen Origins (Terasa-samutthāna)
In the Vibhaṅga it is prescribed for two [cases];
they recite it on the Uposatha day;
I shall explain its origin.
Listen to me according to the knowledge [of the Dhamma]:
the first offense entailing expulsion,
and the second following thereafter.
Matchmaking, repeating [the words of another],
and an extra robe;
wool, and the rule concerning feet.
And by means of an arrangement regarding what has occurred;
the one who confesses a theft, the thief,
and the one not authorized— these are the thirteen.
These methods of origin have been considered by the wise; in each individual method of origin, [the following applies].
Similar cases are seen here.
2.1. The Origin of the First Pārājika:
Sexual intercourse and emission of semen.
The first is undetermined;
it was previously matured,
[committed] in secret with a bhikkhunī.
In the presence of food, in private, and the two [cases of touching];
with a finger, in water, and laughing;
a blow, and indeed vomiting.
And there are fifty-three rules of training (*sekhiya*):
those concerning one who is lustful for the region below the collarbone and above the knees, the polished palm, and the pure [form].
Having completed the rains retreat, she did not follow the instruction of her preceptor.
These are the seventy-six training rules.
Those committed by body and mind are all of a single origin,
just like the first *pārājika*.
The origin of the first *pārājika* is finished.
2.2. The origin of the second *pārājika*:
"What is not given," "sexual intercourse," and "excessive."
The grave offense, for one who desires it herself;
the groundless, the pertaining to another,
the undetermined, and the second [offense].
Taking by force, diverting [alms],
lying, reviling, and slandering;
grave offenses, and digging the earth.
Having realized the truth, he rebuked them.
For the sake of material gain, he had eaten and then driven them out and sprinkled [the ground].
Come, show disrespect and strike fear,
and take away his life;
knowingly perform an act involving living beings.
Living together with one who has fewer years of seniority; complaining against a fellow practitioner;
delusion; and [accusing] without foundation.
Having given a robe that was rightfully obtained,
one might divert it to another person;
why would you take it back at an improper time?
A bad acquisition, and hell;
a group, a classification, and weakness;
a kathina robe and a comfortable dwelling.
One who is fierce in abuse, one who is miserly,
a pregnant woman, and one who is nursing—
these two must undergo training by the Saṅgha for two years.
Three who have gone to lay life,
three who are unmarried maidens,
and those under twelve years of age who are ordained.
Enough for now with this abode of sorrow;
two [rules] concerning consent and the rains-residence;
these are the seventy-first training rules.
The threefold origins have been established:
by body and mind, not by speech;
by speech and mind, not by body.
They arise through three doors,
as in the second *pārājika*.
The exposition of the origin of the second *pārājika* is concluded.
2.3. Originating from Acting as a Matchmaker:
A matchmaker, a hut, a monastery, washing, and receiving.
To offer more than what was requested,
by messenger for both parties,
and two parts of pure silk from Kosiya.
For six years they used a sitting mat;
they neglected both types of money and various other things.
The belt-fastener, the rainy-season robe,
the thread, and the assignment;
the giving of the door and the sewing.
And the pūva-paccaya-jāti:
the jewel, the needle, the bed,
the cotton, the sitting mat, and the itch-scratcher.
Vassikā, and by the Sugata,
viññatti, and añña-cetāpanā;
two for the Saṅgha, and two for a large group.
The person, the light, and the heavy;
the two scraps of food, and the hempen cloth,
and the robe of a recluse.
These fifty-five states arise from six sources:
from the body, not from speech or mind.
Not from speech do body and mind arise;
not from body and speech does the mind arise;
not from body and mind do speech and mind arise.
Not by speech and mind, but by body—
these arise through three doors;
these have six origins.
[She is] similar to one who acts as a go-between.
The origin of the offense of acting as a go-between is finished.
2.4. The Origin of the Formal Rebuke (Samanubhāsanā-samuṭṭhāna).
Schism, following [the schismatic], difficult to correct,
corrupter, grave offense, and wrong view;
consent, loud laughter, and two [others].
And two sounds should not be uttered:
standing on the ground while [the other] is on a low seat,
and [passing] behind or by a by-path.
Following the Vajjis, taking hold, reinstatement, and renunciation;
with whom are the two associated? Two destroyers.
And [the offense] for one who is afflicted;
again, when associated, it is not pacified;
and the invitation ceremony in the monastery.
Every fortnight, the companion, two [robes],
the robe that follows;
these thirty-seven things—
From body, speech, and mind—
all these have a single origin,
just like the formal admonition.
The origin of the *samanubhāsanā* (formal admonition) is concluded.
2.5. The Origin of the *Kathina* (Robe-Privileges):
Three [cases] regarding the *kathina* that has been suspended.
First, alms-food and medicine;
and also urgent and suspicious [medicine],
or two for one who is departing.
Successive dwellings,
not leftover food, an invitation;
a gift from another, [food] from a king, at the wrong time.
And by one who dwells in the forest at will.
Accumulation and hoarding,
before and after [meals], and at improper times;
The five-day transition,
both [types] with the dwelling,
the thigh, and likewise the seat.
These twenty-nine are those that arise through the three doors— body, speech, and mind— but these [remaining] twenty-nine are of body and speech, not of mind.
All [offenses] arising from two origins are the same as those concerning the *kathina*.
The section on the origin of the *kathina* is finished.
2.6. Originating from the Wool of a Ram:
Two kinds of beds, and eating a mouthful [of food] after having already finished.
A group, at an improper time, storing up food;
using tooth-sticks and rags.
An army on march, a battle,
Intoxicants, bathing with water less than a week old,
two [robes] of inferior color,
garlic, attending upon [a layperson], and dancing.
A bathhouse, a carpet, a bed—
both within the kingdom and abroad;
during the rainy season, a pleasure palace.
A couch, spinning thread,
service performed with one's own hands,
and by means of a residence where no monks dwell.
An umbrella, a vehicle, a girdle,
ornaments scented with perfume,
a bhikkhunī, and a trainee nun (sikkhamānā).
A novice nun [offending] against a householder woman;
the offense of being without a chest-wrap: forty-four.
Neither by body nor by speech and mind,
nor by body and mind but by speech—
all [these] have two origins.
"Evenly shorn like wool.
The origin of the offense concerning sheep’s wool is concluded.
2.7. The Origin of the Offense Concerning Verses Recited Together.
Apart from the foot, [the section] on those not authorized,
and likewise on one who has attained final cessation;
two types of low arts are mentioned.
And there is no opportunity for questioning.
These seven training rules [apply] to speech, not to body or mind.
They arise through speech and mind,
but do not arise through the body;
all are originated from two sources.
Similar to the *padasodhamma* [offense].
The section on the origin of the *padasodhamma* is finished.
2.8. Origin of the *addhāna* [offense].
One should gather together the excellent ship for the journey, along with a woman,
and grain when invited.
And eight rules for confession;
these fifteen trainings pertain to the body,
not to speech nor to mind.
They are produced by body and speech;
they are not produced by mind alone.
They are produced by both body and mind.
They do not arise from speech alone;
they originate in four ways: through body, speech, and mind.
They are designated by the Buddha’s knowledge as being equal to the duration of the aeon.
The section on origin by duration is finished.
2.9. Originating from a Band of Thieves:
Listening to a band of thieves, and by requesting soup.
A place covered by night,
and these seven with the "byūha" [formation].
They are born through body and mind.
They do not arise from speech;
they arise through three doors,
and these have two origins.
These offenses originating from a caravan of thieves were taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.
The section on offenses originating from a caravan of thieves is concluded.
2.10. Originating from the Teaching of the Dhamma:
The Tathāgatas do not teach the true Dhamma to one who holds a sunshade in hand.
In the same way, [the merit] of one who holds a staff,
who holds weapons or missiles,
or [provides] sandals, shoes, or a vehicle—
And with the legs folded in the "seyyapallatthikā" posture; wrapped and veiled—
these are the eleven, not fewer.
They are born through speech and mind,
not from the body; all arise from a single source.
Equal in the teaching of the Dhamma.
The origin of the teaching of the Dhamma is finished. 2.11.
The Origin of the Proclamation of Reality (Bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhāna).
A real thing arises through the body,
not through speech nor through the mind;
yet it also originates from speech.
It does not arise from the body, nor from the mind.
It is born of body and speech,
but it is not born from the mind.
That which is called "misrepresentation of what has occurred" arises from three grounds.
The section on the origin of misrepresentation of what has occurred is finished.
2.12. Originating from the Arising of a Thief:
A thief [is defined] by speech and mind;
that does not arise from the body.
It arises through three doors;
this is the offense of theft.
It is uncommitted and has two origins.
Spoken by the Dhamma King.
The origin concerning the theft of a robe is finished.
2.13. The Origin Concerning What is Not Authorized.
That which is not consented to by speech,
nor by body, nor by mind,
arises through body and speech.
That does not arise from the mind alone;
it arises through speech and the mind,
but it does not arise from the body alone.
It arises through three doors;
the fourth base is uncreated.
The section on "Arising Without Consent" is concluded.
For the origin has been well-taught in brief as ten and three;
it is a point that causes non-delusion.
Conducive to the practice of the Netti-dhamma;
the wise one who maintains this does not become deluded when it arises.
The summary of the heads of origins is finished.
